title: Production Patterns: Error Boundaries, Suspense, and Accessibility

subChunks.title: Production Patterns: Error Boundaries, Suspense, and Accessibility
subChunks.hookHtml: The difference between a demo and a production app is resilience and inclusivity. Error boundaries contain failures so one broken component doesn't crash the whole page. Suspense makes async loading states declarative. Accessibility ensures your app works for every user, not just those without disabilities. These are the patterns that separate professional work from playground code.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Error Boundaries

When a component throws during rendering, React unmounts the entire tree by default. Error boundaries catch errors from their children and show a fallback UI instead:

import { Component } from 'react';

class ErrorBoundary extends Component {
  state = { hasError: false, error: null };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    // Log to Sentry, Datadog, etc.:
    console.error('Boundary caught:', error, info.componentStack);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return (
        <div role="alert">
          <h2>Something went wrong.</h2>
          <button onClick={() => this.setState({ hasError: false })}>
            Try again
          </button>
        </div>
      );
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

Vex: "Place error boundaries strategically, not everywhere. A boundary around each major page section prevents one broken widget from taking down the entire page. The goal is resilience at meaningful granularity."

Suspense for async loading

import { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';

const QuestDetailPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/QuestDetailPage'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading page...</div>}>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Accessibility in React — the non-negotiables

Semantic HTML:

// ❌ Not keyboard accessible, not screen-reader announced:
<div onClick={handleSave}>Save</div>

// ✅ Keyboard focusable, announces as button:
<button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>

ARIA labels for icon-only buttons:

<button aria-label="Close modal">✕</button>

Focus management for modals:

const dialogRef = useRef(null);

useEffect(() => {
  if (isOpen) dialogRef.current?.focus();
}, [isOpen]);

// return createPortal(
//   <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" ref={dialogRef} tabIndex={-1}>
//     {children}
//   </div>, document.body);

Accessible form fields:

<label htmlFor="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" aria-describedby="email-hint" />
<p id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</p>

// Error state:
<input
  aria-invalid={!!error}
  aria-describedby={error ? 'email-error' : undefined}
/>
{error && <p id="email-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}

storyBeats.text: Grand Archmage Solomon appears one final time. He doesn't look at the code — he looks at the Lighthouse accessibility report and the error monitoring dashboard.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: A component that throws crashes the page. A page that crashes loses the user. An error boundary is a promise: whatever breaks inside me will not destroy what is outside me. Place them at meaningful boundaries — major page sections, dynamic widgets, anything that fetches data.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Accessibility is not an optional enhancement. An app that only works with a mouse excludes keyboard users, screen reader users, anyone who can't use a pointer. Use semantic HTML. Label every interactive element. Manage focus when modals open. Mark errors with role=alert. These are not extras — they are requirements.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build an accessible, resilient component system:

  • Build an ErrorBoundary class component that shows a fallback with a 'Try again' button when a child throws. Use role="alert" on the fallback.
  • Build a <Modal open onClose children /> that: uses role="dialog" and aria-modal="true"; moves focus to the close button when it opens (useEffect + useRef); renders null when open is false
  • Build a form field with a <label htmlFor> linked to its input, an aria-describedby hint, and an error state that sets aria-invalid and renders a role="alert" paragraph

guidedPracticeTests.label: Form label is linked to input via htmlFor/id

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a fully accessible <Combobox> (searchable dropdown) from scratch. Requirements: a text input with role="combobox" and aria-expanded; a dropdown list with role="listbox"; each option has role="option" and aria-selected; keyboard navigation (Arrow Up/Down cycles through options, Enter selects, Escape closes); focus returns to the input after selection. Wrap in an ErrorBoundary.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three production patterns from this lesson — Error Boundaries, Suspense with lazy loading, and accessibility — to a colleague preparing for a senior React interview. For each: what problem does it solve, how do you implement it, and what breaks if you skip it?

questions.prompt: Why must Error Boundaries be class components rather than function components?
options: They require the getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch lifecycle methods, which have no hook equivalents in React
Error boundaries need access to the class's `this` keyword
React.lazy only works with class components
questions.answer: They require the getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch lifecycle methods, which have no hook equivalents in React
questions.explanation: getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch are class lifecycle methods for catching render-phase errors. As of React 18, there are no hook equivalents. In practice, you write one ErrorBoundary class component and use it everywhere. Libraries like react-error-boundary provide a hook-friendly wrapper.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `React.lazy` combined with `Suspense`?
options: Code splitting — the component's JavaScript bundle is loaded on demand rather than in the initial bundle, reducing time-to-interactive
Lazy evaluation — the component only renders when it first enters the viewport
Suspense pauses the entire app while a component's props are being validated
React.lazy makes a component skip re-renders until its data is ready
questions.answer: Code splitting — the component's JavaScript bundle is loaded on demand rather than in the initial bundle, reducing time-to-interactive
questions.explanation: React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyPage')) tells the bundler to put HeavyPage in a separate chunk. When the component is first rendered, React downloads that chunk asynchronously. Suspense shows the fallback while the download is in progress. Large pages or rarely-visited routes loaded lazily can significantly reduce the initial bundle size.

questions.prompt: A modal opens but focus remains on the button that triggered it. A keyboard user cannot interact with the modal's content. What is the fix?
options: Use useRef on the first focusable element inside the modal and call ref.current.focus() in a useEffect that runs when open becomes true
Add tabIndex={0} to the modal's container div
Use autoFocus on the modal's container div
Set document.activeElement to the modal manually
questions.answer: Use useRef on the first focusable element inside the modal and call ref.current.focus() in a useEffect that runs when open becomes true
questions.explanation: When a modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside it — typically the close button or the first form field. useEffect with the open dependency runs when open changes to true, and ref.current.focus() moves keyboard focus into the modal. Without this, keyboard and screen reader users are stuck.

questions.prompt: A design spec calls for a clickable card that navigates to a detail page. A developer implements it as `<div onClick={navigate('/detail')}>`. What accessibility problems does this create?
options: Keyboard users can't activate it (not in tab order, no Enter/Space handler); screen readers don't announce it as interactive; the purpose is ambiguous to assistive technology
It works correctly — onClick handles all pointer and keyboard events automatically
Only the missing href is a problem — adding role='link' fixes everything
The div needs tabIndex={0} and that alone makes it accessible
questions.answer: Keyboard users can't activate it (not in tab order, no Enter/Space handler); screen readers don't announce it as interactive; the purpose is ambiguous to assistive technology
questions.explanation: A plain div is not focusable by default, not in the tab order, doesn't fire on Enter/Space, and is announced by screen readers as a generic container. The fix: use a real <a href> or <button>. If you must use a div: add tabIndex={0}, role='button' or role='link', and onKeyDown handlers for Enter/Space. Option 1 is always simpler and more correct.
